2._section_summary: This section describes a single study using data from the YouBeauty.com Body Image Survey (YBIS) with respondents from the West (primarily the United States) to examine links between women's body image and subjective happiness. The study measured weight-related body dissatisfaction (actual-ideal weight discrepancy) and body appreciation, and tested a model where education and age shape BMI, which in turn affects body dissatisfaction and body appreciation; those two variables were predicted to affect subjective happiness in opposite directions. The hypothesised model is illustrated in Fig. 1, which reports standardized path coefficients for the US sample.

0.evidence_source: Body appreciation was measured using the Body Appreciation Scale (Avalos et al. 2005), a 13-item scale that measures related dimensions of positive body image.
0._section_summary: This section describes the measure of body appreciation used in the study: the 13-item Body Appreciation Scale (Avalos et al., 2005), rated 1 (Never) to 5 (Always), with overall scores computed as the mean of items. The authors state they omitted non-Western women from the sample and report Cronbach's alphas of .92 for both US and non-US residents. The section does not report sample size, age, BMI, survey method, or correlations with BMI, nor does it label any study as 'Study 1' or indicate multiple studies.

1.evidence_source: "Providing informed consent began the survey on a new page with items of the Body Appreciation Scale."
1._section_summary: This Procedure section describes a single online cross-sectional survey (the YBIS) hosted on YouBeauty.com between September and December 2012; participants provided informed consent online and completed seven webpages of questionnaires. The survey included the Body Appreciation Scale, the Subjective Happiness Scale, and the Photographic Figure Rating Scale, and demographic information was collected on the penultimate page. No sample size, country, demographic breakdowns (age, race, education), BMI assessment method, or correlations are reported in this section.

0.evidence_source: Participants self-reported their height and weight, which we used to calculate their BMI as kg/m2 .
0._section_summary: This section states that participants self-reported their height and weight, which were used to calculate BMI (kg/m2). It also notes that self-reported height and weight are strongly correlated with measured data and valid for identifying relationships in population studies (Spencer et al. 2002). The section does not provide study numbering, sample size, demographics, or details about body appreciation assessment.

1.evidence_source: Third, the accuracy of self-reported data cannot be established in the present instance. For example, although self-reported height and weight are strongly correlated with objectively measured data, there is also a tendency among women to over-report height and under-report their weight (Engstrom et al. 2003).
1._section_summary: This Discussion reports findings from two samples of Western women examining links between body appreciation, body dissatisfaction, BMI, age, and subjective happiness. The authors report that body appreciation strongly predicts subjective happiness and is negatively associated with BMI; limitations include self-selected, online samples and reliance on self-reported height and weight. The section explicitly refers to two samples but does not provide sample sizes or demographic breakdowns.

0._section_summary: This Results section reports descriptive statistics and intercorrelations (Table 2) comparing US and non-US samples. The US sample was significantly older and had higher BMI, whereas educational level proportion was higher in the non-US sample; multigroup SEM showed acceptable-to-good fit with largely identical path coefficients across the two samples and similar standardized effects. The correlation between body appreciation and BMI was −.22 in the US sample and −.17 in the non-US sample (Table 2).
